strengths: Proposes a novel weight-space perspective for bias identification by analyzing the drift of linear-probe weights initialized from text embeddings; this differs from the usual data- or mistake-driven bias discovery pipelines.
The method is conceptually simple and in principle modality-agnostic, leveraging off-the-shelf foundational models, captioning, keyword extraction, and WordNet filtering.
Reports experiments on four datasets spanning vision and text, with improvements in worst-group zero-shot accuracy over several bias-discovery baselines.
Includes qualitative bias lists and some ablation of ranking score and cut-off, plus appendix details on prompts, limitations, and a cosine-similarity bound.
weaknesses: The central claim that weight drift reveals spurious biases is not adequately validated. Weight drift captures any discriminative feature useful for training accuracy, not necessarily an unwanted correlation; the filtering step only removes class-name-related concepts, so legitimate class features can remain and be mislabeled as biases.

The zero-shot prompt-augmentation evaluation is confounded. Using 'max over templates' may include the original/class-only prompt and multiple bias prompts, so gains can arise from test-time prompt ensembling rather than from correctly identified biases. Average accuracy drops substantially on Waterbirds, Nico++, and CivilComments, which is under-discussed and weakens the practical significance.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete. B2T is evaluated only on Waterbirds/CelebA, SpLiCE and Lg only on CelebA, with no comparisons on Nico++ or CivilComments. There is no quantitative bias-discovery metric such as precision/recall against known spurious attributes, and no simple data-only baselines.

The theoretical support is weak. The inequality in Eq. 2 is a reverse triangle inequality and does not establish that high similarity between a concept and a class weight implies the concept causally influences predictions. The min-over-other-classes ranking score is also not well justified and can select concepts that merely disfavor one other class.

Reproducibility and experimental detail are insufficient: no code release or random seeds, unclear exact splits for the custom Nico++ setup and CivilComments, no ablation of the captioning model or keyword extractor, and inconsistent/unclear zero-shot details for the mGTE-based text experiments.

Claims are stronger than the evidence. Describing the method as the 'first' weight-space approach for this problem and claiming 'significant' zero-shot improvement overstates the results, especially given the average-accuracy drops and qualitative, unvalidated 'new bias' candidates. The paper reads as workshop-level rather than a top-tier conference submission in depth and rigor.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting shift in perspective: analyzing the learned weights of a linear probe on top of a frozen foundational model, rather than only inspecting misclassified samples or dataset statistics.

The core idea—initializing classifier weights with class-name embeddings and tracking their drift toward spurious concepts—is simple, intuitive, and potentially applicable across modalities when a joint text-image/text embedding model is available.

The empirical results on Waterbirds and CivilComments show improved worst-group zero-shot accuracy over the reported baseline and some prior bias-identification methods, suggesting the extracted concepts may have practical signal.
The manuscript includes qualitative examples, a small ablation on ranking score and top-q concepts, and brief limitations/broader-impact statements.
The method is clearly described at a high level and could fit into human-in-the-loop bias discovery workflows.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and overclaimed: weight-space probe analysis plus embedding-space concept ranking is a straightforward combination of existing ideas; the claim of being the first weight-space bias-identification method is not well supported or adequately positioned against related interpretability and concept-based work.

The evaluation is indirect and does not convincingly demonstrate bias identification. Zero-shot prompt augmentation with discovered keywords may improve worst-group accuracy through prompt engineering rather than by uncovering true spurious correlations, and the paper lacks controls such as random keywords, class-synonym prompts, or human-verified bias labels.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and inconsistent. Table 1 has many missing entries: B2T is only evaluated on Waterbirds/CelebA, SpLiCE/Lg only on CelebA, and no comparisons are provided on Nico++ or CivilComments, making the claim of significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods unsupported across datasets.

The main results show a problematic worst-group/average trade-off: Waterbirds average accuracy drops from 90.7 to 84.7, and CivilComments average drops from 83.4 to 69.0. The paper does not analyze this trade-off or establish that the method is practically useful for bias mitigation.

Technical soundness is questionable. Eq. 2 is an elementary triangle-inequality bound, is very loose, and is not directly used by the ranking score in Eq. 3. The key assumption that cosine similarity with a concept embedding is high when the concept is present is not validated.

The concept extraction pipeline is noisy and insufficiently analyzed. Captioning models and YAKE keyword extraction can miss or hallucinate concepts, and WordNet filtering only removes class-related terms, not all confounds. There is no precision/recall or error analysis of extracted biases.

Important experimental details are missing or unclear: how many concepts are used, how prompts are selected, whether max-over-templates is standard or test-time tuned, whether results are single-run, and whether hyperparameters were tuned fairly across methods. Table 2 is malformed/incomplete and the ablation is hard to interpret.

The method may discover merely class-correlated words rather than spurious causal features. Without a downstream debiasing experiment or causal validation, the practical significance for bias mitigation remains unclear.

Ethical and fairness concerns are under-addressed. CivilComments experiments use identity and offensive terms such as religious, racial, and sexuality-related keywords in prompts; this risks reinforcing stereotypes, and the broader-impact discussion is generic.

Presentation quality is weak: typos such as 'ConceptShift', grammatical issues, unclear method steps, and poorly formatted figures/tables reduce readability. The related work is thin and does not cover relevant NLP bias-discovery literature.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned, the custom Nico++ subset is not provided, and many design choices around concept filtering and prompt construction are underspecified.

The significance is overstated. The paper claims to 'pin-point unwanted correlations' and reveal 'previously untapped biases,' but provides no quantitative verification that the identified concepts are indeed biases rather than plausible keyword associations.

strengths: Introduces ConceptDrift, a novel weight-space approach for bias identification that analyzes the drift of a linear probe initialized with class-name embeddings, moving beyond data-only or misclassified-sample-based protocols.

The method is intuitive, flexible, and applicable to multiple modalities, demonstrated on image datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++) and a text dataset (CivilComments) using foundation models such as CLIP and mGTE.
Reports consistent improvements in worst-group zero-shot accuracy over baselines including B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg on several datasets, with an ablation study on ranking score and number of concepts.
Provides qualitative bias examples, an appendix with a cosine-similarity bound, and a discussion of limitations and broader impacts.
Paper is generally well written and well organized, with clear figures and a coherent motivation.
weaknesses: The main evaluation of bias quality is potentially circular and unfair: discovered biases are inserted into zero-shot prompts and the best prompt is selected via max over templates. It is not clear whether this selection uses validation or test data; if test data is used, it constitutes test-time tuning and invalidates the comparison. The baseline uses a single prompt while bias-based methods use many candidate prompts, giving an unfair advantage.

Average accuracy often drops substantially (e.g., CivilComments from 83.4 to 69.0), which contradicts the broad claim of significantly improving zero-shot performance. The paper does not adequately discuss this trade-off.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete: not all methods are evaluated on all datasets, and there are no controls for random concepts or matched prompt counts. Standard spurious-correlation discovery methods are not compared.

The number of selected concepts (top-q) is arbitrary, with the authors leaving a principled cut-off strategy for future work. This undermines fully automatic bias identification and raises concerns about hyperparameter tuning on test data.

The theoretical support is limited: the cosine-similarity bound only provides a lower bound under strong assumptions, while the ranking score in Eq. 3 remains a heuristic and is not analyzed for robustness.

Qualitative bias extraction lacks quantitative human validation. Many extracted concepts may be noisy, class-related, or artifacts of the captioning/keyword extraction pipeline rather than genuine spurious correlations.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and important details such as dataset splits, random seeds, and the validation/test protocol for prompt selection are not fully specified.

The novelty is moderate: analyzing linear probe weights and embedding-space concept scores is related to existing interpretability and concept-based methods, and the practical gain over prior bias-discovery approaches is not sufficiently isolated.

strengths: Introduces a novel weight-space perspective for identifying learned spurious correlations, complementing existing data- and error-analysis-based methods. The idea of using drift in linear classification weights relative to class-name embeddings is simple but insightful.

Provides a fairly broad empirical study across modalities: image datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, ImageNet-1k) and a text dataset (CivilComments), with comparisons to B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg where applicable.

The ImageNet-1k qualitative and synthetic validation is compelling: WASP uncovers spurious correlations such as firefighter->Fire Truck and shrimp->American Lobster, and the generated-image experiments show that many strong ImageNet classifiers are fooled by these correlations.

Shows practical utility beyond detection: the proposed SC-based regularization improves worst-group accuracy in fully spurious setups where GroupDRO and ERM struggle, and the zero-shot SC-aware prompting often improves worst-group robustness.

The pipeline is mostly automatic and scalable, with dynamic thresholding, LLM/WordNet-based concept filtering, and an explicit algorithm; code and implementation details are promised, supporting reproducibility.
Addresses an important and timely problem: understanding what a dataset teaches a model, especially for foundation models deployed in high-stakes settings.
weaknesses: The method still depends heavily on the initial concept vocabulary extracted from captions/keywords (GIT, YAKE) and on filtering steps (Llama, WordNet). It cannot identify spurious correlations that are not represented in the extracted concept list, so the departure from data analysis is partial rather than complete.

There is no direct quantitative evaluation of SC detection quality against ground-truth spurious attributes (e.g., precision/recall on Waterbirds or CelebA). Downstream robustness is a useful proxy but does not directly validate each detected correlation, and some results are mixed: CelebA worst-group improvement is marginal, and average accuracy often drops when WASP concepts are used for prompting.

The ImageNet-1k validation is limited to a small number of manually selected scenarios, making it difficult to assess false positives, coverage, and whether the selected examples are representative of WASP's overall output. Synthetic image generation may also introduce artifacts, despite the authors' sanity checks.

The paper analyzes a trained linear probe on frozen embeddings, not full fine-tuning of the foundation model. The abstract and introduction claim to analyze foundation models as they are fine-tuned, but the evidence is mostly for linear probing, which may not capture the same spurious correlations as full fine-tuning.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, such as surpassing all state-of-the-art methods for identifying and naming spurious correlations. Comparisons are also incomplete in places: CivilComments lacks B2T/SpLiCE/Lg baselines, and the regularization comparison omits strong robustness methods such as JTT or DFR.

Presentation clarity could be improved: there are typos, inconsistent terminology (e.g., 'concept-neural'), unclear handling of the CelebA blonde-hair setting, and some notation and thresholding details are difficult to follow without the appendix.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually interesting direction: using the trained classifier weights/linear probe to rank concepts that influence class predictions, as a complement to validation-error or data-frequency based spurious-correlation detection.

Provides striking qualitative and synthetic examples showing that strong pretrained models can be fooled by identified concepts (e.g., firefighter -> Fire Truck, peafowl plus firemen), illustrating a real robustness issue.
Evaluates the approach across multiple modalities and datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, ImageNet), and includes text as well as image experiments.

The proposed dynamic thresholding and class-neutral concept filtering form a practical heuristic pipeline, and the regularization/zero-shot prompt augmentation show some potential utility of the discovered concepts.
The appendix contains detailed concept lists, an algorithm box, and additional ImageNet model results, which aids inspection of the method's outputs.
weaknesses: Core technical mismatch: the method trains only a linear probe on frozen foundation-model embeddings, not the foundation model's own weights. Claims about analyzing 'the model's weights' or 'fine-tuned foundation models' are overstated, and the method cannot detect internal spurious features learned by full fine-tuning.

Concept discovery still depends on data-derived candidate concepts (GIT captions/YAKE keywords/LLM/WordNet filtering). It cannot uncover spurious correlations not expressible in that finite candidate set, undermining claims of transcending data/error analysis.

The ranking score measures class-weight alignment relative to other classes, not a causal effect of the concept on model predictions. Many identified concepts are simply semantically related, confusable, or noisy (e.g., 'osprey' for Bald Eagle, 'kettle kettle' for Coffeemaker), so filtering may confuse class co-occurrence with spuriousness.

ImageNet validation relies on synthetic FLUX images generated from prompts chosen after knowing the spurious correlations. It lacks evaluation on real ImageNet or natural held-out data, so generator artifacts, prompt selection bias, and OOD composition effects are not ruled out.

There is no quantitative detection benchmark for spurious-correlation identification. Table 4 is a qualitative comparison without precision/recall, human validation, coverage, or significance analysis, and many CivilComments concepts are generic or typo-prone (e.g., 'solly').

Mitigation evaluations are weak: zero-shot prompting on CivilComments improves worst-group accuracy but substantially reduces average accuracy (80.2 -> 71.0), Celeba gains are tiny (72.8 -> 73.1), and no baselines are provided on CivilComments.

The 'fully spurious setup' is artificial and may not reflect realistic causal structure. The regularization may act as a generic regularizer rather than specifically correcting spurious correlations, and CelebA improvements are small with high variance.

Missing ablations and sensitivity analyses: concept extraction method, GIT/YAKE/LLM/WordNet filtering, initialization, threshold sensitivity, random-concept prompting, hyperparameters (r, alpha), and negative spurious correlations are not adequately studied.

The paper overclaims that it 'surpasses all state-of-the-art methods', 'covers all trainset samples', and works 'fully automated at scale', while the evidence is mostly indirect, qualitative, or limited to a few generated examples.

Reproducibility and clarity issues: the code URL is missing in the manuscript, data are promised only upon acceptance, notation and equations are sometimes not fully specified, and there are typos/malformed references.

strengths: Introduces a novel weight-space perspective for detecting spurious correlations, moving beyond data-only or error-based analysis toward the model's decision mechanism.
Evaluates the approach across multiple modalities and datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, ImageNet), which strengthens the empirical breadth.
Provides a practical pipeline with concept extraction, class-neutral filtering, scoring, and dynamic thresholding, plus code availability.
Includes validation through synthetic image generation and demonstrates that many ImageNet classifiers can be fooled by the discovered concepts.
Shows meaningful improvements in some settings, especially Waterbirds worst-group accuracy and CivilComments worst-group accuracy under zero-shot prompt augmentation.
Clearly discusses fairness scope and avoids overclaiming in that specific direction.
weaknesses: The method analyzes only the final linear classification layer trained on frozen foundation-model embeddings, not the foundation model's own weights. This conflicts with the paper's framing of detecting spurious correlations learned by fine-tuned foundation models and limits the scope of the claims.

The ImageNet validation may not isolate dataset-induced learned spuriousness: the generated prompts explicitly include concepts strongly associated with the induced class (e.g., firemen/fire truck, shrimp/American lobster, newspaper/crossword), so models may rely on general semantic associations rather than spurious correlations learned from ImageNet.

The claim of surpassing all state-of-the-art methods is not consistently supported: Table 5 shows average accuracy drops on CelebA and CivilComments, and improvements on CelebA are marginal. Several baselines are missing for CivilComments and ImageNet.

The method relies on many heuristics and hyperparameters (YAKE concepts, LLM/WordNet filtering, dynamic thresholding, modality-gap correction), but ablations and sensitivity analyses are limited. The dynamic thresholding rule is ad hoc and not theoretically justified.

The fully spurious setup is insufficiently detailed and may be circular or synthetic: WASP-discovered concepts are used to regularize against WASP-discovered spuriousness, without independent ground-truth validation of the discovered correlations.

Reproducibility is incomplete: full ImageNet concept lists, false-positive/recall analysis, compute costs, seeds, and statistical significance tests are missing. Some qualitative concepts appear noisy or off-topic, suggesting precision issues in the pipeline.
The paper overstates the novelty and generality of the weight-space approach, since the analyzed weights belong to a linear probe rather than the underlying foundation model.
